OMG finally the analyses

2026-05-27

We will finally analyse this data properly, and bring all datasets together… But there’s been changes to figures! So we gotta get creative.

We need to clean up a bit for the new files, and define color scales:

I looked at the GWAS Catalog’s description of their ancestry curation, and I still don’t know what to do with the samples that Amanda has, because I would argue that this is genetic ancestry, poorly described, which is not necessarily the case for the other two datasets. But it also has a bunch of terms that are clearly racial in origin and inspiration, so, like… dunno what to do here.

unique(dbGapFinal$variable) # This is really a horrible mix of both, but I guess primarily of geography terms, so I'm making it a new colour scheme... Set 3 here we go
## [1] Other                            HispanicB                       
## [3] Other Asian or\nPacific Islander European                        
## [5] African American                 HispanicA                       
## [7] South Asian                      East Asian                      
## [9] African                         
## 9 Levels: African African American East Asian European HispanicA ... South Asian
dbGapFinal$variable <- factor(dbGapFinal$variable, levels = c("African", "African American", "European", "South Asian", "East Asian", "Other Asian or\nPacific Islander", "HispanicA", "HispanicB", "Other"))

dbGapColours <- brewer.pal(9,"Set3") 

scale_color_dbGap <- function(...){
    ggplot2:::manual_scale('color', 
        values = setNames(dbGapColours, levels(dbGapFinal$variable)), 
    )
}

scale_fill_dbGap <- function(...){
    ggplot2:::manual_scale('fill', 
        values = setNames(dbGapColours, levels(dbGapFinal$variable)), 
    )
}

Razi et al colours:

These are basically ours, but smaller - we gotta reorder his factor levels so they match well. Both final and clean have been merged with his, so we gotta create factor levels for both.

allSRAFinal <- allSRAFinal %>% 
  mutate(pred_pop = paste0("1KG-", pred_pop, "-like")) %>%
  mutate(pred_pop = gsub("1KG-NA-like", "", pred_pop))

allSRAClean <- allSRAClean %>% 
  mutate(pred_pop = paste0("1KG-", pred_pop, "-like")) %>%
  mutate(pred_pop = gsub("1KG-NA-like", "", pred_pop))

allSRAFinal$pred_pop <- factor(allSRAFinal$pred_pop, levels = c("1KG-AFR-like", "1KG-EUR-like", "1KG-SAS-like", "1KG-EAS-like", "1KG-AMR-like", "")) 
allSRAClean$pred_pop <- factor(allSRAClean$pred_pop, levels = c("1KG-AFR-like", "1KG-EUR-like", "1KG-SAS-like", "1KG-EAS-like", "1KG-AMR-like", "")) 

martinColors <- c('#9C8DC3', '#DB6968', '#60BC55', '#4D97CD', '#F8984E')
kasperColors <- darken(martinColors, 0.25)

# NA is grey50
scale_fill_kasper <- function(...){
    ggplot2:::manual_scale('fill',  
        values = setNames(c(kasperColors, 'grey50'), levels(allSRAFinal$pred_pop)), 
    )
}

scale_color_kasper <- function(...){
    ggplot2:::manual_scale('color',  
        values = setNames(c(kasperColors, 'grey50'), levels(allSRAFinal$pred_pop)), 
    )
}

SRA and manual colours:

# First let's fix Sub-Saharan and set the unknowns to NA so we don't break the plots.
litRevFinal <- litRevFinal %>% 
  mutate(finalGeo = gsub("Subsaharan Africa", "Sub-Saharan Africa", finalGeo)) %>%
  mutate(finalGeo = gsub("Unknown", NA, finalGeo)) %>%
  mutate(finalRace = gsub("Unknown", NA, finalRace))

litRevFinal$finalGeo <- factor(litRevFinal$finalGeo, levels = c("Sub-Saharan Africa", "Europe", "South Asia","East Asia", "Asia (NOS)"))

scale_fill_geography <- function(...){
    ggplot2:::manual_scale('fill',  
        values = setNames(c('#9C8DC3', '#F3D78A', '#DB6968', '#60BC55', '#BCCC45', '#4D97CD', '#04C3C8', '#C69C3A', '#F8984E', '#8B96AD', '#FBC9C4'), levels(allSRAFinal$strictestGeography)), 
    )
}

scale_color_geography <- function(...){
    ggplot2:::manual_scale('color',  
        values = setNames(c('#9C8DC3', '#F3D78A', '#DB6968', '#60BC55', '#BCCC45', '#4D97CD', '#04C3C8', '#C69C3A', '#F8984E', '#8B96AD', '#FBC9C4'), levels(allSRAFinal$strictestGeography)), 
    )
}

raceColours <- brewer.pal(8,"Set2") #8 because we don't plot NAs

scale_color_race <- function(...){
    ggplot2:::manual_scale('color', 
                           values = setNames(raceColours, levels(allSRAFinal$strictestRace)), 
    )
}

scale_fill_race <- function(...){
    ggplot2:::manual_scale('fill', 
        values = setNames(raceColours, levels(allSRAFinal$strictestRace)), 
    )
}

# And finally, the world Bank Economic region palette, for later:
wberCols <- c(viridis::turbo(n = 7))
scale_fill_wber <- function(...){

}

We’re also going to use some additional info from the World Bank, so let’s add those columns in now, to all datasets (they’re already in allSRAFinal, so only need to add them to allSRAClean, dbgap, which is easy—all USA—and to the recount manual files):

Worth keeping in mind that China here includes Hong Kong SAR, which is world bank high income while the rest of China is upper middle.

worldBank <- read.csv("World_Bank_Descriptors.csv")

dbGapFinal$worldBank <- "High income"
dbGapFinal$worldRegion <- "North America"

# Lit review has the unique benefit of being the only place where we have submitting country and sampling country, so we will consider both

litRevFinal <- litRevFinal %>%
  mutate(samcountry = gsub("England", "United Kingdom", samcountry)) %>%
  mutate(samcountry = gsub("Hong Kong", "China", samcountry)) %>%
  mutate(lacountry = gsub("Hong Kong", "China", lacountry)) %>%
  mutate(samcountry = gsub("United States; United States", "United States", samcountry)) %>%
  mutate(samcountry = gsub("Pennsylvania", "United States", samcountry)) %>%
  mutate(samcountry = gsub("^Unknown$", "Unreported/Unknown", samcountry)) %>%
  mutate(samcountry = gsub("^Unreported$", "Unreported/Unknown", samcountry)) %>%
  mutate(samcountry = gsub("^unreported$", "Unreported/Unknown", samcountry))

litRevFinal$worldBankSample <- worldBank[match(litRevFinal$samcountry, worldBank$Economy),]$Income.group
litRevFinal$worldBankLA <- worldBank[match(litRevFinal$lacountry, worldBank$Economy),]$Income.group

litRevFinal$worldRegionSample <- worldBank[match(litRevFinal$samcountry, worldBank$Economy),]$Region
litRevFinal$worldRegionLA <- worldBank[match(litRevFinal$lacountry, worldBank$Economy),]$Region

litRevFinal %>% count(samcountry, worldBankSample)

# As before, missing countries are all high income, so we can set them to that manually now that we're happy with the names:
litRevFinal <- litRevFinal %>% 
  mutate(worldBankLA = if_else(grepl("South Korea|Taiwan", lacountry), "High income", worldBankLA)) %>%
  mutate(worldRegionLA = if_else(grepl("South Korea|Taiwan", lacountry), "East Asia & Pacific", worldRegionLA)) %>%
  as.data.frame()

# And now we need to clean up some labels so we can plot them better. Good thing is, it's just an ampersand:
litRevFinal$worldRegionLA <- gsub("& ", "&\n", litRevFinal$worldRegionLA)
litRevFinal$worldRegionSample <- gsub("& ", "&\n", litRevFinal$worldRegionSample)

litRevFinal <- litRevFinal %>%
  mutate(hasDescriptor = if_else(grepl("ancestry", ReportedS), "Geographic", "Racial"))

# And now the fun one... allSRAClean:
# Some names need to be fixed, but others are more flexible? I'd rather have USA than United States.
allSRAClean$finalCountry <- gsub("^UK$", "United Kingdom", allSRAClean$finalCountry) 
allSRAClean$finalCountry <- gsub("^Korea$", "South Korea", allSRAClean$finalCountry)
allSRAClean$finalCountry <- gsub("^The Netherlands$", "Netherlands", allSRAClean$finalCountry)

allSRAClean$worldBank <- worldBank[match(allSRAClean$finalCountry, worldBank$Economy),]$Income.group
allSRAClean %>% count(finalCountry, worldBank) %>% filter(is.na(worldBank))
##   finalCountry worldBank      n
## 1    Hong Kong      <NA>    848
## 2         Iran      <NA>     71
## 3        Macao      <NA>    184
## 4       Russia      <NA>   1416
## 5  South Korea      <NA>   6023
## 6       Taiwan      <NA>   1468
## 7         <NA>      <NA> 292071
# Plenty of NAs to fix, but some countries have annoying names in World Bank, so we mix and match. ... 
allSRAClean <- allSRAClean %>%
  mutate(finalCountry = gsub("Hong Kong|Macao", "China", finalCountry)) %>% # Hong Kong and Macao are part of China 
  mutate(worldBank = ifelse(grepl("Iran|China", finalCountry), "Upper middle income", worldBank)) %>%
  mutate(worldBank = ifelse(grepl("Taiwan|South Korea|Russia", finalCountry), "High income", worldBank))

  # And now the regions they define:
allSRAClean$worldRegion <- worldBank[match(allSRAClean$finalCountry, worldBank$Economy),]$Region
allSRAClean %>% count(finalCountry, worldRegion) %>% filter(is.na(worldRegion))
##   finalCountry worldRegion      n
## 1         Iran        <NA>     71
## 2       Russia        <NA>   1416
## 3  South Korea        <NA>   6023
## 4       Taiwan        <NA>   1468
## 5         <NA>        <NA> 292071
allSRAClean <- allSRAClean %>%
  mutate(worldRegion = ifelse(grepl("Iran", finalCountry), "Middle East & North Africa", worldRegion)) %>%
  mutate(worldRegion = ifelse(grepl("Taiwan|South Korea", finalCountry), "East Asia & Pacific", worldRegion)) %>%
  mutate(worldRegion = ifelse(grepl("Russia", finalCountry), "Europe & Central Asia", worldRegion))

dbGapCountry <- dbGapFinal %>% drop_na(finalCountry) %>% group_by(finalCountry, worldRegion, worldBank) %>% summarise(value = sum(value)) %>% mutate(db = "dbGaP") %>% as.data.frame()
## `summarise()` has grouped output by 'finalCountry', 'worldRegion'. You can
## override using the `.groups` argument.
# This one is needed for the supplement, but not for the main figure, so we gotta split allCountry into 2
litRevCountry <- litRevFinal %>% drop_na(lacountry) %>% group_by(lacountry, worldRegionLA, worldBankLA, samcountry, worldRegionSample, worldBankSample, hasDescriptor) %>% summarise(value = sum(individs)) %>% mutate(db = "Manual") %>% as.data.frame()
## `summarise()` has grouped output by 'lacountry', 'worldRegionLA',
## 'worldBankLA', 'samcountry', 'worldRegionSample', 'worldBankSample'. You can
## override using the `.groups` argument.
names(litRevCountry)[1:3] <- c("finalCountry", "worldRegion", "worldBank")

# But this is all very annoying because it makes the plots by country and we get a lot of weird artefacts in our plots. So let's do a bit more merging of data before we plot

allCountryMain <- rbind.fill(sraCountry, sraCountryStrict, dbGapCountry, litRevCountry)
allCountryMain <- allCountryMain %>%
  mutate(worldBank = gsub("middle ", "middle\n", worldBank)) %>% 
  mutate(worldBankSample = gsub("middle ", "middle\n", worldBankSample)) %>%
  mutate(hasDescriptor = if_else(grepl("dbGaP", db), "GrafPop", hasDescriptor)) %>%
  mutate(finalCountry = if_else(grepl("USA", finalCountry), "United States", finalCountry))

allCountry <- allCountryMain %>% filter(db %in% c("dbGaP", "SRA05"))
allCountryAlt <- allCountryMain %>% filter(db %in% c("dbGaP", "SRA"))

# But we want to organise the plotting of worldBank by factor levels, so:
allCountry$worldBank <- factor(allCountry$worldBank, levels = c("High income", "Upper middle\nincome", "Lower middle\nincome"))
allCountryAlt$worldBank <- factor(allCountryAlt$worldBank, levels = c("High income", "Upper middle\nincome", "Lower middle\nincome"))

How overrepresented are these numbers? We begin by grabbing the UN population data and doing some more mergers - important to note that we add back the manual review data here because otherwise it would need a figure of its own:

worldPop <- read.csv("RNA-seq-diversity_world-population.csv")
worldPop$name <- gsub("Korea, South", "South Korea", worldPop$name)

allCountry2 <- allCountryMain %>% 
  group_by(finalCountry, db, worldRegion) %>% 
  summarise(value = sum(value)) %>%
  as.data.frame()
## `summarise()` has grouped output by 'finalCountry', 'db'. You can override
## using the `.groups` argument.
allCountry3 <- left_join(allCountry2, worldPop, join_by( "finalCountry" == "name"))

# Only one NA: Turkey, which is not current in the UN numbers:
allCountry3[allCountry3$finalCountry %in% "Türkiye",]$value.y <- worldPop[worldPop$name %in% "Turkey (Turkiye)",]$value
allCountry3[allCountry3$finalCountry %in% "Türkiye",]$region <- worldPop[worldPop$name %in% "Turkey (Turkiye)",]$region

# And now we get some fancy new columns for plotting
allCountry3 <- allCountry3 %>% 
  mutate(fractPop = value.y/sum(worldPop$value)) %>%
  group_by(db) %>%
  mutate(fractDB = value.x/sum(value.x)) %>%
  mutate(excess = fractDB/fractPop) %>%
  as.data.frame()

ggplot(allCountry3, aes(x = excess, y=finalCountry, color=db)) +
  geom_point(size = 3) +
  scale_x_continuous(trans='log10', breaks = trans_breaks("log10", function(x) 10^x), labels = scales::comma) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 1) +
  annotation_logticks(sides="b") +
  xlab("Overrepresentation in database\nrelative to global population") +
  ylab("Depositing institution country") +
  theme_bw(base_size = 8) +
  theme(legend.title.align = 1, legend.direction = "horizontal", legend.background=element_blank(), legend.position="bottom")

# This one is for the reviewers...

# Let's quickly do a test for how many studies and samples come from HIC relative to all studies, given in the text as 74:
hicStudyTest <- allSRAClean %>% drop_na(strictCountry) %>% group_by(worldBank) %>% 
  summarise(studies = n_distinct(SRA.Study)) %>% 
  mutate(prop = studies/sum(studies)) %>% as.data.frame()
binom.test(hicStudyTest[hicStudyTest$worldBank %in% "High income",]$studies, sum(hicStudyTest$studies), 0.74)
## 
##  Exact binomial test
## 
## data:  hicStudyTest[hicStudyTest$worldBank %in% "High income", ]$studies and sum(hicStudyTest$studies)
## number of successes = 5781, number of trials = 6609, p-value <
## 0.00000000000000022
## alternative hypothesis: true probability of success is not equal to 0.74
## 95 percent confidence interval:
##  0.8664939 0.8826064
## sample estimates:
## probability of success 
##              0.8747163
# Finally, now that we have countries, we can look at who deposits from where, with some charming alluvial plot:
allSRAClean <- allSRAClean %>%
  mutate(
    repo = ifelse(grepl("^SR", SRA.Study), "SRA", ifelse(grepl("^ER", SRA.Study), "ENA", "DRA")))

# Alluvial plots and prep for the manual data only:
# For labelling, 10 most common depositing countries:
top10Countries <- allSRAClean %>% drop_na(strictCountry) %>% count(strictCountry) %>% slice_max(n, n = 10) %>%  pull(strictCountry)

repoAlluvial <- allSRAClean %>% drop_na(strictCountry) %>% 
  count(strictCountry, repo, worldRegion)

ggplot(data = repoAlluvial, aes(axis2 = repo, axis1 = strictCountry, y = n)) +
   scale_x_discrete(limits = c("Depositing Country", "Depositing Repo"), expand = c(.2, .05)) +
   geom_alluvium(aes(fill = worldRegion)) +
   scale_fill_wber() +
   geom_stratum(width = 1/5) +
   ylab("Samples") +
   geom_text_repel(stat = "stratum", 
                   aes(label = after_stat(ifelse(stratum %in% top10Countries | x == 2, as.character(stratum), ""))), 
                   direction = "y", 
                   size = 2.5,
                   nudge_x = 0.3,
                   segment.size = 0.3,
                   segment.color = "grey50",
                   min.segment.length = 0) +
   theme_minimal(base_size = 8) +
   theme(legend.position = "none")

ggsave("repository_alluvial_for_reviewers.pdf", width = 5, height = 5)
ggsave("repository_alluvial_for_reviewers.png", width = 5, height = 5)

And now we’re making a map with all of this…

toplot<-aggregate(BioSample~strictCountry,data=allSRAClean,FUN=length)
colnames(toplot) <- c('name','samples')
toplot$name[which(toplot$name=='United States')] <- 'United States of America'
toplot$name[which(toplot$name=='UK')] <- 'United Kingdom'
toplot$name[which(toplot$name=='Korea')] <- 'South Korea' #???
toplot$name[which(toplot$name=='Türkiye')]<- 'Turkey'

toplot2 <- ne_countries(scale='medium', returnclass = 'sf') %>%
  left_join(toplot, by = 'name')
toplot2$samples[which(is.na(toplot2$samples))]<-0

# check for any that failed to merge
toplot$name[-which(toplot$name %in% toplot2$name)] 
## character(0)
tmp<-subset(toplot2,samples>0)
table(tmp$income_grp) # Note that this is older than world bank data and doesn't include the split between lower middle and upper middle, which makes Tanzania show up as low income here
## 
##    1. High income: OECD 2. High income: nonOECD  3. Upper middle income 
##                      29                       8                      14 
##  4. Lower middle income           5. Low income 
##                       5                       1
ggplot(data=toplot2) +
  geom_sf(aes(fill=log10(samples)), color='grey', size=0.1) +
  coord_sf(crs = "+proj=eqearth +wktext") +
  scale_fill_viridis(option="rocket", na.value = "grey50", direction=-1) +
  theme(panel.grid.major = element_line(linewidth = 0.25, linetype = 'solid', color = "grey"),
        panel.border = element_blank(),
        axis.text.x=element_blank(),
        axis.ticks.x=element_blank()
  )

# We wanna test the USA, so:
usaSamples <- allSRAClean %>% filter(strictCountry == "United States") %>% nrow()
allSamples <- allSRAClean %>% drop_na(strictCountry) %>% nrow()
usaProp <- allCountry3[allCountry3$finalCountry %in% "United States" & allCountry3$db %in% "SRA" , ]$fractPop[1]

# And finally, a binomial test for the USA
binom.test(usaSamples, allSamples, usaProp)
## 
##  Exact binomial test
## 
## data:  usaSamples and allSamples
## number of successes = 232251, number of trials = 425231, p-value <
## 0.00000000000000022
## alternative hypothesis: true probability of success is not equal to 0.04244169
## 95 percent confidence interval:
##  0.5446782 0.5476733
## sample estimates:
## probability of success 
##              0.5461761
# We also want to test this against the proportion of samples from the USA in microbiome studies, which we cite in the text as being 40%
binom.test(usaSamples, allSamples, 0.4)
## 
##  Exact binomial test
## 
## data:  usaSamples and allSamples
## number of successes = 232251, number of trials = 425231, p-value <
## 0.00000000000000022
## alternative hypothesis: true probability of success is not equal to 0.4
## 95 percent confidence interval:
##  0.5446782 0.5476733
## sample estimates:
## probability of success 
##              0.5461761
# And another one for institutions in LATAM + Caribbean
latamSamples <- allCountry3 %>% filter(worldRegion == "Latin America &\nCaribbean" & db == "SRA") %>% 
  summarise(samples = sum(value.x)) %>%
  mutate(proportion = samples/allSamples)

# But to do the test we need to know how many people live in LATAM... 
latamProp <- worldPop %>% filter(region %in% c("Central America and the Caribbean", "South America")) %>% summarise(sum(value))/sum(worldPop$value)
            
binom.test(latamSamples$samples, allSamples, latamProp[1,1])
## 
##  Exact binomial test
## 
## data:  latamSamples$samples and allSamples
## number of successes = 509, number of trials = 425231, p-value <
## 0.00000000000000022
## alternative hypothesis: true probability of success is not equal to 0.06654691
## 95 percent confidence interval:
##  0.001095308 0.001305576
## sample estimates:
## probability of success 
##            0.001196996
#And some stats on the Razi et al subset:
allSRAClean %>% drop_na(pred_pop) %>% filter(missingness %in% c("(0,10]", "(10,20]", "(20,30]")) %>% count(pred_pop) %>% mutate(freq = n/sum(n))

allSRAClean %>% drop_na(pred_pop) %>% filter(missingness %in% c("(0,10]", "(10,20]", "(20,30]")) %>% summarise(studies = n_distinct(SRA.Study), samples = n_distinct(BioSample))
##   studies samples
## 1    3540  105166
allSRAClean %>% drop_na(pred_pop) %>% summarise(studies = n_distinct(SRA.Study), samples = n_distinct(BioSample))

## 1   12291  747964

And one final check… the agreement in country assignment between our two methods.

finalCountries <- allSRAFinal %>% count(SRA.Study, finalCountry) # 248 rows because one study is deposited from multiple sites

finalCountries %>% group_by(SRA.Study) %>%
  filter(n() > 1)

## Warning in left_join(finalCountries, cleanCountries, join_by("SRA.Study" == : Detected an unexpected many-to-many relationship between `x` and `y`.
## ℹ Row 3 of `x` matches multiple rows in `y`.

# And now we tabulate:
compareCountries %>%
  mutate(strictCountry = gsub("United States", "USA", strictCountry)) %>%
  group_by(SRA.Study, finalCountry) %>%
  summarise(
    has_match = any(!is.na(strictCountry) & strictCountry == finalCountry),
    has_mismatch = any(!is.na(strictCountry) & strictCountry != finalCountry),
    has_na = any(is.na(strictCountry)),
    n.x = first(n.x),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) %>%
  mutate(category = case_when(
    has_match & !has_mismatch & !has_na ~ "full match",
    has_mismatch & !has_match & !has_na ~ "full mismatch",
    has_na & !has_match & !has_mismatch ~ "all NA",
    has_match & has_na & !has_mismatch ~ "match + NA",
    has_mismatch & has_na & !has_match ~ "mismatch + NA",
    TRUE ~ "other"
  )) %>%
  group_by(category) %>%
  summarise(n_studies = n(), total_n.x = sum(n.x))

Bearing this in mind we actually want to compare country of deposition of all studies vs country of deposition of studies with metadata. This is inherently noisy (116:21 above) but what can you do?

allSamplesClean <- allSRAClean %>% drop_na(strictCountry) %>% count(finalCountry) %>% mutate(finalCountry = gsub("United States", "USA", finalCountry))
allSamplesFinal <- allSRAFinal %>% count(finalCountry)

sampleRep <- left_join(allSamplesClean, allSamplesFinal, by = c("finalCountry"))
sampleRep <- sampleRep %>% mutate(
  n.y = ifelse(is.na(n.y), 0, n.y),
  frac = n.y/n.x)

ggplot(sampleRep, aes(y = finalCountry, x = frac)) +
  geom_bar(stat = "identity") +
  ggtitle("Fraction of deposited samples with\npopulation descriptor metadata") +
  xlab("") +
  ylab("Depositing country") +
  # scale_fill_wber() +
  # theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust=1)) +
  theme(legend.title.align = 1, legend.direction = "horizontal", legend.background=element_blank(), legend.justification = c(0,0), legend.position="bottom")

ggsave("samples_with_metadata.pdf", width=3, height=5)
ggsave("samples_with_metadata.png", width=3, height=5)

geographyProp <- allSRAFinal %>% drop_na(strictestGeography) %>% count(strictestGeography) %>% mutate(freq = n/sum(n))
raceProp <- allSRAFinal %>% drop_na(strictestRace) %>% count(strictestRace) %>% mutate(freq = n/sum(n))

# These two are calculated here because they're used below. They have to be remade for plotting because of how the script was structured, but YOLO..
litRevGeoProp <- litRevFinal %>% drop_na(finalGeo) %>% group_by(finalGeo) %>% summarise(n = sum(individs)) %>% mutate(freq = n/sum(n)) 
litRevRaceProp <- litRevFinal %>% drop_na(finalRace) %>% group_by(finalRace) %>% summarise(n = sum(individs)) %>% mutate(freq = n/sum(n))

dbgapProp <- dbGapFinal %>% group_by(variable) %>% summarise(n = sum(value)) %>% mutate(freq = n/sum(n))

raziProp <- allSRAClean %>% drop_na(pred_pop) %>% filter(missingness %in% c("(0,10]", "(10,20]", "(20,30]")) %>% count(pred_pop) %>% mutate(freq = n/sum(n))

# And then we want to know about concordance between Razi et al and author-reported descriptors.
confMatrix <- allSRAFinal %>% drop_na(pred_pop) %>% drop_na(strictestGeography) %>% filter(missingness %in% c("(0,10]", "(10,20]", "(20,30]")) %>% count(strictestGeography, pred_pop)

df_cm <- melt(confMatrix)
## Using strictestGeography, pred_pop as id variables
df_cm$Percentage <- round(100 * df_cm$value / sum(df_cm$value), 1)

df_cm <- df_cm %>% group_by(pred_pop) %>% mutate(percentGA = round(100 * value/sum(value), 1))
df_cm <- df_cm %>% group_by(strictestGeography) %>% mutate(percentRep = round(100 * value/sum(value), 1))

# Reverse the order of Predicted factor levels for pretty plotting:
df_cm$pred_pop <- factor(df_cm$pred_pop, levels = rev(unique(df_cm$pred_pop)))

Working out the overrepresentation of countries in the datasets, so I can make that second supplementary plot. We grab the population regions from the toplot2 object Amanda had as a good starting point:

worldPop <- left_join(worldPop, toplot2[,c(19,93:96)], by = "name") 
worldPop <- worldPop[,-8]

worldPopNA <- worldPop[is.na(worldPop$subregion),]
worldPopOk <- worldPop %>% filter(!is.na(subregion))

worldPopNA <- worldPopNA %>%
  mutate(subregion = ifelse(grepl("America", region), "Americas", subregion)) %>%
  mutate(subregion = ifelse(grepl("Australia and Oceania", region), "Oceania", subregion)) %>%
  mutate(subregion = ifelse(grepl("Europe", region), "Europe", subregion)) %>% 
  mutate(subregion = ifelse(grepl("Middle East", region), "North AF and WA", subregion)) %>%
  mutate(subregion = ifelse(grepl("Africa", region), "Sub-Saharan Africa", subregion)) %>%
  mutate(subregion = ifelse(grepl("Korea, North|Macau|Paracel", name), "East Asia", subregion)) %>%
  mutate(subregion = ifelse(grepl("Burma", name), "Southeast Asia", subregion)) 

worldPop2 <- rbind(worldPopNA, worldPopOk)

… and we stop there until we work out what to do with all the Europeans outside Europe!

Lol the internet suggested just adding the number of Europeans outside Europe, and the best source I could find was the Wikipedia page on the European diaspora (at least I saved it to Zotero. Technically should be able to read in those numbers and, uh, substract them from the countries, and recompute stuff? But that is such BS…)

I removed overseas holdings of European countries to avoid double counting (Ceuta, Melilla, New Caledonia, etc), and also countries that the world bank says are European (Russia, one of the stans)

euros <- read.csv("20240901_European_diaspora_data.csv")
africans <- read.csv("20240901_African_diaspora_data.csv")

# Let's drop the mixed ones? I don't know what to do with them... If I don't I end up double-counting a LOT of Brazilians
euros <- euros %>% filter(!grepl("mixed", Note))
africans <- africans %>% filter(!grepl("mixed", Note)) %>%
  mutate(Country = ifelse(grepl("Turkey", Country), "Turkey (Turkiye)", Country))

worldPop3 <- left_join(worldPop2, euros, join_by("name" == "Country") )
worldPop3 <- left_join(worldPop3, africans, join_by("name" == "Country") )

worldPop3 <- worldPop3 %>%
  mutate(European = ifelse(is.na(European), 0, European)) %>%
  mutate(African = ifelse(is.na(African), 0, African)) %>%
  mutate(nonEuroPop = value - European) %>% 
  mutate(nonAFR = value - African) %>%
  mutate(noneither = value - European - African)

# This also needs a bit more cleaning:
regionalPop <- regionalPop %>%
  mutate(subregion = gsub("Northern Africa|Western Asia", "North AF and WA", subregion)) %>%
  mutate(subregion = ifelse(grepl("Africa", subregion), "Sub-Saharan Africa", subregion)) %>%
  mutate(subregion = ifelse(grepl("Europe", subregion), "Europe", subregion)) %>%
  mutate(subregion = ifelse(grepl("America", subregion), "Americas", subregion)) %>%
  mutate(subregion = gsub("Australia and New Zealand|Melanesia|Micronesia|Polynesia", "Oceania", subregion)) %>%
  mutate(subregion = gsub("Caribbean", "Americas", subregion)) %>%
  mutate(subregion = gsub("South-Eastern Asia", "Southeast Asia", subregion)) %>%
  mutate(subregion = gsub("Eastern Asia", "East Asia", subregion)) %>%
  mutate(subregion = gsub("Southern Asia", "South Asia", subregion)) %>%
  mutate(subregion = gsub("North AF and WA", "North Africa and\nWestern Asia", subregion)) %>%
  group_by(subregion) %>% summarise(population = sum(population), euro = sum(euro), noneuro = sum(noneuro), afr = sum(afr), nonafr = sum(nonafr), others = sum(others))

# And now we're finally ready to compare things!
regionalPop2 <- regionalPop %>%
  mutate(euro = ifelse(grepl("Europe", subregion), population - afr, euro)) %>%
  mutate(afr = ifelse(grepl("Sub-Saharan Africa", subregion), population - euro, afr)) %>%
  mutate(global = ifelse(grepl("Sub-Saharan Africa", subregion), sum(afr), others)) %>%
  mutate(global = ifelse(grepl("Europe", subregion), sum(euro), global)) %>%
  mutate(fractPop = global/sum(global)) %>%
  mutate(sanityCheck = euro + afr + global - population)

  mutate(excess = freq/fractPop)

# And then yet another binomial test, this time checking if the proportion of samples in the manual is a similar draw to the SRA:
eurSRAprop <- allGeoProps %>% filter(db == "SRA") %>% filter(strictestGeography == "Europe") %>% summarise (freq = freq)
eurLitHits <- allGeoProps %>% filter(db == "Manual") %>% filter(strictestGeography == "Europe") %>% summarise (freq = n)
litRevTotals <- litRevFinal %>% filter(!is.na(finalGeo)) %>% summarise(inds = sum(individs))
binom.test(eurLitHits[1,1], litRevTotals[1,1], eurSRAprop[1,1])

## 
## data:  eurLitHits[1, 1] and litRevTotals[1, 1]

## alternative hypothesis: true probability of success is not equal to 0.5560543
## 95 percent confidence interval:
##  0.5009957 0.5446146
## sample estimates:
## probability of success 
##              0.5228377
# And to GWAS data (90.5% per GWAS monitor on 2025.06.29)
binom.test(geographyProp[geographyProp$strictestGeography %in% "Europe",]$n, sum(geographyProp$n), 0.905)

## 0.00000000000000022

## 95 percent confidence interval:
##  0.5461524 0.5659228
## sample estimates:
## probability of success 
##              0.5560543
# Now the plot:
ggplot(allGeoProps, aes(x = excess, y=strictestGeography, color=db)) +
  geom_point(size = 3) +
  # scale_x_continuous(trans='log2', breaks = trans_breaks("log2", function(x) 2^x), labels = trans_format("log2", math_format(2^.x))) +
  scale_x_continuous(trans='log2', breaks = trans_breaks("log2", function(x) 2^x)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 1) +
  # annotation_logticks(sides="b") +
  xlab("Fold overrepresentation in database\nrelative to global population") +
  ylab("Geographic/Ancestral descriptor") +
  theme_bw(base_size = 8) +
  theme(legend.title.align = 1, legend.direction = "horizontal", legend.background=element_blank(), legend.position="bottom")

ggsave("global_overrepresentation.pdf", width = 3, height = 5)
ggsave("global_overrepresentation.png", width = 3, height = 5)

Let’s move onto the US census, which is a lot easier

uscensus <- read.csv("RNA-seq diversity - SI tables v2 - US census.csv") 

# To make the merges work:
uscensus <- uscensus %>%
  mutate(Race = gsub(" alone", "", Race)) %>% 
  mutate(Race = ifelse(is.na(Race), "Hispanic", Race)) %>%
  mutate(Race = gsub("and ", "and\n", Race)) %>% 
  mutate(Race = gsub("or ", "or\n", Race)) %>%
  mutate(Race = gsub("\nOther", "\nother", Race)) %>%
  mutate(Race = gsub("More than 1 race", "Multiple", Race)) %>%
  mutate(Race = gsub("Some Other Race", "Other", Race))

raceProp <- left_join(raceProp, uscensus, join_by("strictestRace" == "Race"))
litRevRaceProp <- left_join(litRevRaceProp, uscensus, join_by("finalRace" == "Race"))

raceProp$db <- "SRA"
litRevRaceProp$db <- "Manual"
names(litRevRaceProp)[1] <- "strictestRace"
 
allRaceProps <- rbind(raceProp, litRevRaceProp)
allRaceProps$excess <- allRaceProps$freq/allRaceProps$Proportion.of.the.population

# Another test comparing litrev and SRA same as above:
whiteSRAprop <- allRaceProps %>% filter(db == "SRA") %>% filter(strictestRace == "White") %>% summarise (freq = freq)
whiteLitHits <- allRaceProps %>% filter(db == "Manual") %>% filter(strictestRace == "White") %>% summarise (freq = n)
litRevTotals <- litRevFinal %>% filter(!is.na(finalRace)) %>% summarise(inds = sum(individs))
binom.test(whiteLitHits[1,1], litRevTotals[1,1], whiteSRAprop[1,1])
## 
##  Exact binomial test
## 
## data:  whiteLitHits[1, 1] and litRevTotals[1, 1]
## number of successes = 763, number of trials = 1250, p-value =
## 0.000000001836
## alternative hypothesis: true probability of success is not equal to 0.6906429
## 95 percent confidence interval:
##  0.5827321 0.6375473
## sample estimates:
## probability of success 
##                 0.6104
# And now excess in White and Other:
binom.test(raceProp[raceProp$strictestRace == "White",]$n, sum(raceProp$n), raceProp[raceProp$strictestRace == "White",]$Proportion.of.the.population)
## 
##  Exact binomial test
## 
## data:  raceProp[raceProp$strictestRace == "White", ]$n and sum(raceProp$n)
## number of successes = 9669, number of trials = 14000, p-value <
## 0.00000000000000022
## alternative hypothesis: true probability of success is not equal to 0.5783619
## 95 percent confidence interval:
##  0.6829114 0.6982950
## sample estimates:
## probability of success 
##              0.6906429
binom.test(raceProp[raceProp$strictestRace == "Other",]$n, sum(raceProp$n), raceProp[raceProp$strictestRace == "Other",]$Proportion.of.the.population)
## 
##  Exact binomial test
## 
## data:  raceProp[raceProp$strictestRace == "Other", ]$n and sum(raceProp$n)
## number of successes = 162, number of trials = 14000, p-value <
## 0.00000000000000022
## alternative hypothesis: true probability of success is not equal to 0.005098315
## 95 percent confidence interval:
##  0.009866261 0.013483865
## sample estimates:
## probability of success 
##             0.01157143
ggplot(allRaceProps, aes(x = excess, y=strictestRace, color=db)) +
  geom_point(size = 3) +
  # scale_x_continuous(trans='log2', breaks = trans_breaks("log2", function(x) 2^x), labels = trans_format("log2", math_format(2^.x))) +
  scale_x_continuous(trans='log2', breaks = trans_breaks("log2", function(x) 2^x)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 1) +
  # annotation_logticks(sides="b") +
  xlab("Fold overrepresentation in database\nrelative to US population") +
  ylab("US Census Term") +
  theme_bw(base_size = 8) +
  theme(legend.title.align = 1, legend.direction = "horizontal", legend.background=element_blank(), legend.position="bottom")

ggsave("us_census_overrepresentation.pdf", width = 3, height = 5)
ggsave("us_census_overrepresentation.png", width = 3, height = 5)

Much easier…

And now, remaking the plot of samples by study across SRA and dbGaP

sampleGeography <- allSRAFinal %>% count(SRA.Study, strictestGeography) %>% drop_na(strictestGeography)
sampleRace <- allSRAFinal %>% count(SRA.Study, strictestRace) %>% drop_na(strictestRace)
meltSampleGeography <- melt(sampleGeography)
## Using SRA.Study, strictestGeography as id variables
meltSampleRace <- melt(sampleRace)
## Using SRA.Study, strictestRace as id variables
geobyStudy <- ggplot(meltSampleGeography, aes(x = strictestGeography, y=value,fill=strictestGeography)) +
  geom_boxplot(width=0.8, outlier.shape = NA) +
  geom_jitter(size=0.8, width=0.2, color="#333333") +

dbGapbyStudy <- dbGapFinal %>% filter(value > 0) %>%

# Alluvial plots and prep for the manual data only:
litRevCountry <- litRevFinal %>% drop_na(lacountry) %>% group_by(lacountry, worldRegionLA, worldBankLA, samcountry, worldRegionSample, worldBankSample, hasDescriptor) %>% summarise(value = sum(individs)) %>% mutate(db = "Manual") %>% as.data.frame()
## `summarise()` has grouped output by 'lacountry', 'worldRegionLA',
## 'worldBankLA', 'samcountry', 'worldRegionSample', 'worldBankSample'. You can
## override using the `.groups` argument.
# Fix a couple of names for litRev so we can do some nice stacked bar plots...

 mutate(worldBank = gsub("middle ", "middle\n", worldBank)) %>%
 mutate(worldBankSample = gsub("middle ", "middle\n", worldBankSample)) %>%
 mutate(finalCountry = if_else(grepl("USA", finalCountry), "United States", finalCountry))

 ggplot(data = ., aes(axis1 = worldRegion, axis2 = worldRegionSample, y = value)) +

   geom_text(stat = "stratum", aes(label = after_stat(stratum)), size=2.5) +
   theme_minimal(base_size = 8) +

And then, of the studies we looked at manually, how often did we fail to get metadata for them despite it existing? This is the raw dump from the survey, so it’s messy and not worth thinking about too hard, but the individual studies are in there…

rawLitRev <- read.table("20260301_recount3_RNA-seq_diversity_Form_Responses.tsv", header=T, sep="\t", fill=T, comment.char = "")

names(rawLitRev)[2] <- "SRA.Study"
noLitData <- setdiff(rawLitRev$SRA.Study, litRevFinal$recount3)

intersect(noLitData, unique(allSRAFinal$SRA.Study)) # None! Tada! We are done!
## character(0)
